result: The study tested 614 commercial antibodies against 65 neuroscience-related proteins using standardized knockout cell line validation across three applications (WB, IP, IF). More than 50% of antibodies failed in one or more applications, yet 50-75% of proteins were covered by at least one high-performing antibody depending on application, with recombinant antibodies outperforming monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C2-C27 and C95-C98 provide comprehensive methodological details and quantitative results from systematic testing. The experimental design using isogenic WT/KO cell pairs with standardized protocols across 614 antibodies provides robust evidence. Performance criteria are clearly defined (C95-C98), sample sizes are substantial, and results are consistently reported across multiple applications with specific success rates.

result: Analysis of the Antibody Registry database shows that 53% of human proteins are covered by at least five renewable antibodies, while ~15% have no renewable antibodies available. In the tested set of 65 proteins, well-performing renewable antibodies were found for 77% (WB), 75% (IP), and 54% (IF) of targets.
evaluation: Claims C28-C36 present database analysis and experimental coverage data with specific percentages. The Antibody Registry data (C28-C31) is properly cited, and experimental results (C32-C36) are consistent with the methodology described. The coverage rates across different applications are quantitatively reported and align with the overall study design.

result: Recombinant antibodies (67% WB, 54% IP, 48% IF success rates) consistently outperformed monoclonal (41% WB, 32% IP, 31% IF) and polyclonal antibodies (27% WB, 39% IP, 22% IF) across all three applications tested.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 provide clear quantitative comparisons across antibody types with specific success rates for each application. The data are internally consistent and support the conclusion of superior recombinant antibody performance. However, C42 appropriately notes this could reflect enhanced internal characterization by suppliers rather than inherent superiority, showing appropriate scientific caution.

result: Success in immunofluorescence (IF) is the best predictor of antibody performance in Western blot (WB) and immunoprecipitation (IP) applications.
evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by statistical analysis using the McNemar test shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The chi-square statistics demonstrate significant correlations between IF success and performance in other applications (p<0.005 for IF-IP, p<0.0005 for IF-WB), while WB-IP correlation was not significant (p>0.1).

result: Comparison of manufacturer recommendations to knockout validation revealed that genetic validation strategies (89% WB, 80% IF confirmation) substantially outperformed orthogonal validation strategies (80% WB, 38% IF confirmation). Additionally, 37% of antibodies not recommended for IP by manufacturers successfully enriched their targets.
evaluation: Claims C44-C56 provide systematic comparison of validation methods with clear quantitative outcomes. The data demonstrate that genetic strategies are more reliable than orthogonal approaches, particularly for IF (38% vs 80% confirmation). The finding that many unrecommended antibodies perform well in IP (C47) is well-documented. Sample sizes are adequate for the comparisons made.

result: Following characterization, manufacturers withdrew 73 antibodies from the market and changed recommendations for 153 antibodies out of 409 antibodies with conflicting data, representing more than half of underperforming antibodies being reassessed.
evaluation: Claims C57 and C7 report manufacturer responses to the validation data with specific numbers. The data show concrete actions taken (73 withdrawn, 153 modified recommendations from 409 conflicting antibodies), demonstrating real-world impact. This represents 55% of conflicting antibodies being addressed (226/409), supporting the claim of "more than half."

result: Bibliometric analysis using CiteAb revealed that 31% of WB publications, 35% of IP publications, and 22% of IF publications used antibodies that failed validation in this study. Extrapolating these findings suggests 20-30% of figures in the literature may be generated using antibodies that do not recognize their intended targets.
evaluation: Claims C58-C63 present bibliometric data showing substantial use of underperforming antibodies in published literature. While the citation tracking methodology using CiteAb is reasonable, the extrapolation to "20-30% of figures in the literature" (C63) is speculative and depends on whether the 65-protein sample is representative of the broader proteome. The authors appropriately qualify this with "if our results are representative," but generalizability remains uncertain without broader sampling.

result: The optimal antibody validation methodology uses wild-type and isogenic CRISPR knockout cells, with estimated costs of $25,000 per protein or $50 million for the entire human proteome. This cost is substantially below the estimated $1 billion/year wasted on poor-quality antibodies.
evaluation: Claim C11 is well-supported by citations and the current study's methodology. Cost estimates (C12, C68, C69) are clearly stated as estimates based on the authors' experience. The comparison to waste estimates (C70) appropriately cites prior work (Voskuil et al., 2020). While cost estimates involve assumptions about scaling and industrialization, they provide reasonable order-of-magnitude projections for planning purposes.

result: The 65-protein sample represents a heterogeneous mix of well-studied (23% with >500 publications) and poorly-studied proteins (77% with 37-498 publications). More than half of protein targets were covered by well-performing renewable antibodies, suggesting it might be possible to identify reagents for half the human proteome by mining commercial collections.
evaluation: Claims C72-C78 provide quantitative characterization of the protein sample and coverage rates with specific data from NIH database searches and experimental results. The extrapolation to the human proteome (C79-C80) is appropriately qualified as speculative ("might be possible") and acknowledges limitations (only 27% of manufacturers represented). The heterogeneity of the protein sample strengthens the generalizability argument.

result: Despite superior performance of recombinant antibodies in all applications tested, their uptake by the scientific community has been unsatisfactory, with polyclonal antibodies remaining the most purchased. The study argues that future antibody generation programs should focus on recombinant technologies.
evaluation: Claims C81-C90 combine established knowledge about polyclonal antibody limitations (C81-C82, properly cited), current market trends (C84-C86), and experimental findings from this study (C89). The recommendation for recombinant technologies (C90) logically follows from the performance data. Claims about market trends and community uptake are presented as general knowledge but align with cited literature (Gray et al., 2020).

result: Using knockout or knockdown strategies to screen antibodies for their intended application provides the most effective approach to identify selective antibodies. A major barrier to large-scale antibody validation is the lack of available knockout cell lines, and creation of a broadly accessible biobank of knockout cells for each human gene should be a priority.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 present logical recommendations based on the study's findings about validation method effectiveness (particularly C43, C52-C56). The identification of knockout cell line availability as a barrier (C92) follows from the practical experience of the study. The recommendation for a biobank (C93) is a reasonable infrastructure proposal to address this limitation.

result: Antibody characterization data are disseminated through the RRID community via the Antibody Registry, RRID Portal, and participating manufacturers' websites, with all 65 reports gathered on ZENODO under the YCharOS community following technical peer review.
evaluation: Claims C64, C26, and C27 describe the data dissemination infrastructure with specific platforms and URLs. The integration with existing resources (Antibody Registry, RRID Portal) and open access publication on ZENODO are verifiable. The peer review process by scientific advisors from academia and industry adds quality control. This represents a well-designed data sharing strategy.

result: Many commercial antibodies do not recognize their intended targets, with approximately 1.6 million antibodies targeting 96% of human proteins. An estimated $0.375-$1.75 billion is wasted yearly on non-specific antibodies, and poor-quality antibodies are a major factor in the reproducibility crisis.
evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C10 establish the context and motivation for the study. C1 represents established field knowledge. C8-C10 are properly supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Bandrowski et al., 2023; Baker, 2015; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Voskuil et al., 2020; Baker, 2020). These claims accurately represent prior work and provide appropriate context.

result: The partnership includes 10 companies representing approximately 27% of antibody manufacturing worldwide.
evaluation: Claim C13 provides a factual statement about the study partnership composition. While the method for calculating the 27% market share is not detailed, this is a verifiable factual claim about the study design. The limitation that only 27% of manufacturers are represented is appropriately acknowledged throughout the manuscript when discussing generalizability.

result: The validation process robustly identifies antibodies that fail to recognize their intended targets, and removal of poorly performing products will have significant impact. The project provides a tremendous resource that will result in significant improvements in rigor and reproducibility.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 and C94 present conclusions about the study's effectiveness and impact. C65 is supported by the comparative testing strategy showing that failures are evident when other antibodies perform well. C66 logically follows from the bibliometric data (C58-C62). C94 is a reasonable concluding statement about expected impact, though actual long-term impact on reproducibility remains to be demonstrated.
